items.question: How do you see the role of online programming resources in helping someone like you enter computer science?
items.object: The internet’s role in making programming and informatics competitions accessible
items.answer: My introductory teacher was not involved in competitions; he simply taught computers, so our county high school had no resources for getting started with this. But because there were online judges and public resources online, I began teaching myself programming and competing then. After learning for a while, in my second year of high school—I had started relatively late—I entered NYP, the provincial competition. What I remember clearly is that I did not pass the preliminary round, but later I went along as the third person—or tagged along—to attend the final provincial event. Not the provincial selection, but the competition within the province. In the end I got second prize. The next year, in my senior year, I got first prize. I basically taught myself all of it. That period had a great impact on my later choice to follow the computer-science path. It also made me feel that, because of the internet, it could let us access information relatively freely. It allowed someone like me—a grassroots contestant, so to speak—to gradually enter this field. I think that’s really amazing.

items.question: How do you understand Professor Yu Yong’s advice to be modest as a person but bold in your work?
items.object: Being modest as a person but bold in one's work
items.answer: In college, especially during the ACM experience, Professor Yu Yong emphasized to us: be modest as a person, but bold in your work. I think that had a great influence on us. And indeed, in my career I have met all kinds of people. I have found that, first, you need edge when you do things: when you are completing something, you have to be ambitious, right? But in the meantime, most of the factors that enable you to accomplish something come not from yourself alone. Among the people I have met, the lesson I learned from them is that they are humble. They are all very humble and know that, in many cases, you need people around you to work together to accomplish something. Starting from that premise, I think communication with people requires a certain degree of respect and a willingness to say, let’s collaborate together. But also in the meanwhile, that does not mean we should not be very ambitious, or that we should not challenge the status quo.

items.question: What did your experience applying restricted Boltzmann machines to ImageNet teach you about choosing research problems and methods?
items.object: Choosing research problems and methods: the ImageNet project and KDD Cup experience
items.answer: Looking back, in that first research project, no one told me, first, how to do it, or second, what problems I might encounter. The obvious mistake now is this: we thought ImageNet was a newly emerged, excellent, important problem. That was correct, because good research requires choosing important problems. We also thought deep learning was important, and that a seemingly sound statistical method was the restricted neural network, the restricted Boltzmann machine. So we said, okay, let us try it and make these two things work—use that method on ImageNet. But in research, it is hard for your judgment to be so precise that you choose both the right problem and the right method on the first try. We essentially persisted for two years with the right problem and the wrong method. In the end, it turns out it’s not good. When we later did KDD, we partly learned from that experience. Starting from restricted Boltzmann machines, we examined the problem and found that matrix factorization would work better, so we began working on matrix-factorization methods. In the end, that experience was why we got good KDD results. If we had used only one method, I do not think we could have achieved those results.

items.question: How did you come to understand the importance of choosing research problems?
items.object: Choosing research problems
items.answer: I feel that when you first teach yourself, the training you most readily get is how to solve a problem, right? For example, in a course project, the problem is simple: you have a major assignment, the goal is clearly defined, and you solve it. But research has another important stage: how do you choose a problem? What problem do you work on, and what method do you use to solve it? Looking back now, the problem we chose was not bad—solving ImageNet was not a bad problem—but early in my research career I barely knew what other problems I could solve. I remember a turning point: Professor Li Hang came to APEX and gave a talk. Before that, we were basically unguided and I was exploring on my own. Professor Li gave a talk saying, “In spam detection, there are this problem, this problem, and this problem; this is how we solve them.” I realized, hey, I could solve all these problems, and I could think of other methods. There were other problems in the world besides the one I had been looking at. I became very excited, followed Professor Li Hang, and was fortunate to receive support from Professor Li Hang and Professor Yang Qiang to intern in Hong Kong for a period. Then I began to know what problems we could look at and solve. That was a very major change.

items.question: How have you developed your preference for problem-first research in machine learning?
items.object: Problem-first research and the motivation for working on machine-learning systems
items.answer:
First, I have come to see very clearly that there are different research styles. One starts from methods: I become the leading figure in a direction and can apply my method in all kinds of places. The other is that I am interested in a class of problems and try different methods to solve them. At least my years of experience have made me realize I belong to the latter. I am interested in creating things. At the very beginning, wanting to make games myself was also about hoping to create something. Machine learning is the same: creating intelligence and creating things is an original motivation. Based on that, I realized we probably cannot keep choosing only what method to work on.

After I began machine learning, I found that many of my bottlenecks came from whether I could scale things up—make them run large and fast. I remember clearly when ImageNet had just broken through, my advisor, others, and I all wondered: why did it work? Was it because of neural networks? We thought perhaps it was not necessarily neural networks; perhaps the reason was a relatively large hypothesis space and a large amount of data that could be scaled up. Neural networks are still very important because they have a large parameter space. But we wanted to challenge that hypothesis. If you could use massive data with other model types, could that work? Because I had previously worked on KDD, I had the bias that tree models were strong. Could we make tree models work? And my advisor thought: could we do kernel methods? In the end I still thought tree models were better, so I chose the tree-model path.

Then I found that a major bottleneck was systems: when doing tree models, the existing tools could not compute the model I wanted quickly enough. Once I realized this—this is no longer a very controversial view; everyone now knows AI depends on data, compute, and algorithms, right?—I saw that, when we first began machine learning, most attention was on algorithms. From a problem-first perspective, systems were a bottleneck, and I do not like having a problem simply blocked by a bottleneck so I cannot continue. So I thought, okay, should we solve it? That gradually led me into machine-learning systems.

items.question: What did building XGBoost teach you about what it takes to make a machine-learning system successful?
items.object: Building XGBoost as a complete machine-learning system
items.answer: Looking back now, I think an important point is that the ACM experience taught us to take something to the extreme. I think that is extremely important: take something to the extreme. So once we began this because of that opportunity, I tried every possible way to see whether we could make it a bit faster, then faster still. When we released it, it was the fastest thing in the world for the gradient-boosting method. Another point is that, because I do algorithm research, XGBoost contains some detailed algorithmic work that allows it to work out of the box on many problems. For example, one very important feature is missing values. In many machine-learning settings, there are missing values. Someone whose data I rely on may not tell you their age, gender, or other information. In traditional machine learning, you first clean the data, replacing missing values with a median or something else. But I thought the model could itself infer how to handle missing values. XGBoost has this built in: if a value is missing, it decides how to categorize it based on historical missing-value patterns. This was extremely popular because people do not want to solve missing values themselves. So, because we took something to the extreme and made it work, this was the first time I felt that you need to look at a vertical problem. If you are building a machine-learning system, doing only algorithms or only systems cannot bring complete success. You have to know how the algorithm can advance and how the system can be built.

items.question: How do you now assess the judgments that led you to pursue tree models for gradient boosting?
items.object: The judgments behind pursuing tree models for gradient boosting
items.answer: First, I think one judgment we made at the time was correct: a model’s capacity should not be constrained. The reason we chose tree models was very simple, because with tree models you can grow them arbitrarily. With ordinary models, you set a fixed number of parameters—for example, a linear regression with 100 parameters has 100 parameters; you cannot grow it arbitrarily. A very strong property of tree models is that, as your data volume increases, you can arbitrarily grow the depth, right? That property is extremely powerful. At the time, we did not think neural networks could not do this, because neural networks are tensile. But what initially—and ultimately—surprised me was that neural networks achieve this through another, more brute-force approach: instead of trying to grow my parameter space, I simply make my parameter space very large from the outset. That was somewhat surprising. But tree models having this property is also why we did not choose kernel methods, because I felt kernel methods did not fully have this property. Of course, although non-parametric methods can indeed grow in width with the amount of data, they do not have this particular property of tree models. And I think another correct judgment we made about tree models was that they are still extremely strong on tabular data. At least even now, for tabular data and time series, out-of-the-box models, tree models are still almost everyone’s go-to tools. The reason is also that they can use splitting and composition to do things that ordinary models—including neural networks—find difficult to do directly. So I think that is something that we kind of did right. One thing we did not really anticipate, which later also became obvious, was that another very strong property of neural networks is their compositionality. You can have different modules, such as Transformer blocks and linear blocks, which can be combined with one another, allowing their expressive power to represent things much more compactly through composition. Relatively speaking, we did know this at the time—for example, I knew convolutional networks did have this ability, because I had worked on deep learning before—but we were trying to test the hypothesis of whether model representation or data volume was more important, right? We wanted to test that hypothesis, and that is what motivated that project.

items.question: How did AlexNet’s success change your willingness to try building a deep-learning framework again?
items.object: AlexNet’s success and the motivation for CXXNet
items.answer: I had had that not-so-successful experience with deep learning before, but I had always had a strong passion for deep learning, right? Then after seeing that AlexNet had succeeded, I thought, hey, maybe deep learning really was the right thing after all; maybe we could try it. So we used the not-so-successful experience from my graduate-school period to start building a new deep-learning framework, called CXXNet. I built the first version with Bin Xu, who is now at Nvidia. At the time, Caffe had already been released by Yangqing. For CXXNet, we developed a technology called expression templates. Through template programming, when you write update rules—for example multiplication and subtraction—you can compress them into one template and generate an inlined GPU kernel. At the time we thought this could make it simpler to build a deep-learning framework, so we built it.

items.answer: We gathered together and discussed whether we should jointly build a project that could absorb lessons from Minerva. In the Caffe era, everyone’s core code was in C++; Minerva had this Python-first implementation. So we said, OK, let’s build this together. The core ideas were: first, we felt we should be Python-first, so you could write deep-learning frameworks in Python. Second, we wanted automatic scheduling: when you directly write forward and backward functions in Python, it can use your computation dependencies to allow parallelism across multiple cards—for example, AllReduce, with communication and computation proceeding together—through automatic scheduling. Third, it could do automatic differentiation. In the first generation of deep-learning frameworks, such as Caffe, there was backpropagation; in the second generation, there was automatic differentiation through computation graphs. That is very different, and the leap made a major improvement to systems optimization. So we decided to do this project together. And because Mu Li had been working on PS, parameter servers, distributed support also needed to be a first-class citizen. So we started: OK, we could build this together. The name MXNet probably came from Minerva and CXXNet—it was called MixNet, since everyone was mixing together, including the mixed programming style itself. At the time, it was clear that there would be different programming styles: what people now call declarative—declare a computation graph—and programming, where you write it and it computes directly, right? MXNet’s path was to mix them, supporting both.

items.question: How do you look back on the design process behind VTA, the Versatile Tensor Accelerator you developed during TVM’s early work?
items.object: The design process and programmability of VTA, the Versatile Tensor Accelerator
items.answer: I think it was a process of constant iteration. And what was interesting was, again, that we were not afraid even though we did not understand. For example, when we were building the NPU, our initial idea may have been wilder: could we directly bake the neural network into the wires of the FPGA? Of course, people later worked in that direction too, through HLS, high-level synthesis. But later we concluded, OK, let’s first make an NPU. The TPU paper had just come out, but nobody knew what TPU was like. So, OK, we would design an NPU ourselves. When we were designing it, if you looked directly at the problem, you would see the issues. For example, we found an obvious issue with NPUs: memory reads and writes and computation must happen simultaneously. At first we thought: how do we solve this? In general, one instruction reads memory and one instruction computes. How can you, at the hardware level, make compute instructions and memory-read instructions overlap through pipelining or some other method? And although we did not realize it at the time, we later found that our NPU design was very interesting. Most early NPUs were entirely hardware—meaning they were completely unprogrammable. An NPU had no instructions; it just performed one function: convolution, right? Something went in and something came out. But the NPU we designed, called VTA, Versatile Tensor Accelerator, had an instruction set. Because we started from a compiler perspective, you could decompose matrices or other operations into smaller steps, smaller matrices, and memory reads and writes, then program more operators using one instruction set. So to make a set of programmable microinstructions plus overlap possible, we designed it from first principles, despite my not having a systems-architecture background. items.question: How do you understand the differences among GPUs, TPUs, and NPUs today?
items.object: The distinctions and convergence among GPUs, TPUs, and NPUs
items.answer: I think the distinction is becoming increasingly blurred now. GPUs originally came from graphics programming, but CUDA has evolved to the point that it basically no longer has much to do with graphics programming. It is purely what is called S-SAME, single instruction multiple thread: you can program with many threads, right? Generally, TPUs and NPUs can be regarded as a similar category. They have relatively complex instruction sets, so one instruction can read a block of memory, or one instruction can perform a relatively large matrix operation. Generally, an NPU may not have a notion of threads, because some of its instructions are themselves very large. But now GPUs and NPUs are moving toward each other. For example, NVIDIA has introduced things like tensor cores, which originally were the kind of thing only NPUs had, right? And many NPUs may introduce notions of threads to get closer to the CUDA ecosystem. So today the boundary is much blurrier.

items.answer: I think to do interesting things is often necessarily uncomfortable. items.question: How do you see the next stage of TVM’s development as a machine-learning compiler project?
items.object: TVM’s future direction in machine-learning compilation
items.answer: First, in doing the TVM project, I brought a very different mindset, because I hoped it could evolve. That is, if you look at TVM now and its form at the beginning, we have almost gone through several iterations to better adapt to the latest things we have seen. But in my view, the problem itself still exists. We still have a very large problem: it still takes enormous engineering effort to deploy a machine-learning model—now, large models—across various devices. On the one hand, models have become more homogeneous. But conversely, models are not that homogeneous, and the hardware itself has become harder; every generation of GPU has a different programming model. In my view, this problem is far from solved. And people have now begun to reach a consensus that compiler technology needs to be one part of this, right? So for TVM itself, what we hope to do now is continue simplifying this process—not even merely providing a solution itself, but enabling a compiler for a vertical domain to be built quickly. For example, in previous years we used TVM to build WebLLM and MLC, so that we could compile deep-learning large language models directly onto the web, web pages, and devices such as in-vehicle devices. I think these are directions we are working to develop in the future: continuing to reinvent the technology itself. Of course, there are unknowns, because it is difficult to see a project reinvent itself, innovate on its own, and then continue moving forward. So there are certainly unknowns. But I think it remains an interesting problem, and especially now it is a more interesting problem. With AI agents and all kinds of DSLs appearing, we are continuing to work in this area. And another thing to note is that we need to integrate better with the broader ecosystem. This means that, for example, we have recently been trying to separately abstract some shared parts, such as basic function-call conventions, so that calls can be made more easily between PyTorch, JAX, and other frameworks. I hope to see continued integration with the whole ecosystem, alongside breakthroughs in some vertical domains. Ultimately, I hope that even deep-learning compilation, which is still not so simple, can become as easy as writing a neural network. Writing a neural network is already very simple—you can do it in Python in just a few lines—so I have always hoped to see machine-learning engineering development become similarly simple.

items.question: How do you understand the role of machine-learning systems in the breakthroughs of the big-data era?
items.object: Machine-learning systems in the big-data era
items.answer: These systems have always played a very large role in the breakthroughs of AI and machine learning as a whole. Looking back over roughly the past twenty years, I think machine learning has gone through several major breakthroughs. The first can be seen as the arrival of the big-data era. That was when machine learning moved from textbooks into recommendation systems. A highly emblematic event was Netflix’s Netflix Challenge, a recommendation-system competition. Then there were later companies such as ByteDance, right? Toutiao initially got started by relying on recommendation systems. At that time, one major breakthrough came from data volume: from working with a few hundred data points to data on the scale of hundreds of millions, marking the emergence of big data. At that time, you find that earlier non-open-source systems—such as the large-scale linear regression used for Baidu’s Fengchao, built early on by Mu Li, Wen Yuan, and others—as well as open-source systems like Apache Spark and XGBoost, all belonged to the big-data era. You see that the tools of the big-data era made it possible for everyone to use the data, right?

items.question: How do you understand the role of machine-learning systems in enabling the deep-learning pattern-recognition breakthrough?
items.object: Machine-learning systems in the deep-learning pattern-recognition breakthrough
items.answer: I regard this as the deep-learning pattern-recognition breakthrough. A major reason it was initially possible was that Alex Krizhevsky was a very strong hacker. CUDA ConvNets initially used, I think, two GPUs, and trained for a week. At the time that was unimaginable—our machine-learning experiments usually took minutes, right? Being willing to spend a week on something, and doing multi-GPU optimization and parallelism, was different. Later, Caffe greatly drove the adoption of deep learning in computer vision; Yangqing and his team made an enormous contribution. Then frameworks such as MXNet, PyTorch, and TensorFlow came later. There is a clear contrast: when I first started doing deep-learning projects, to make a model we had to spend six months writing perhaps 20,000 lines of CUDA. Once deep-learning frameworks appeared, you could complete the same thing almost in minutes by writing a few lines of Python. That was a huge technological innovation. It was precisely because of that innovation that we could conduct far more algorithmic exploration on top of those frameworks.

items.question: How do you see MLC LLM's role in advancing deep-learning compilation?
items.object: MLC LLM and its role in developing deep-learning compilers
items.answer: MLC LLM is actually an extension of TVM, because we realized that to build a deep-learning compiler, we must understand very clearly where the problems are. items.question: How do you think convergence toward a few dominant models will affect the importance of ML systems research?
items.object: The future importance of ML systems research as models converge
items.answer: I think it is possible that the community could decline; you cannot completely rule out that possibility, right? On the other hand, what is interesting now is that hardware itself has to be specialized, because we can no longer solve problems through generality alone. Each generation of chips advances in a very different way in order to achieve efficiency. And you will find that the software for every generation of chips, even software from the same vendor, almost always needs to be adapted again for some new features. This means the complexity comes from two sides: one is the complexity of support for the hardware itself, and the other is the complexity of model iteration. The current strong need for specialization means these two complexities move further forward together. Models are gradually converging toward being hardware-friendly. But to make hardware and models work together, their entanglement will become increasingly apparent. Yet because there is no simple recipe that can get you the next 2x, everyone also needs to be creative, in some sense. At that point, problems arise: the solution for the next generation of hardware will differ from that for this generation, and the model best suited to the next generation of hardware may also differ from the model best suited to this one. We can see DeepSeek designing for its application scenario and hardware environment in order to achieve optimal efficiency. From that perspective, I think this is very interesting. It may instead be a reason why taking a more systematic view of ML systems will become more important going forward.

items.question: How do you view the apparent convergence of deep learning models in light of the hardware lottery?
items.object: Model convergence, the hardware lottery, and diversity in deep learning
items.answer: Although models appear to have converged, you find that it still takes effort to bring up different new model variants. And finally, this returns us to a topic called the hardware lottery: hardware itself constrains the possibilities for how models can develop, which causes models to converge too, but perhaps not into the optimal form, right? So for the field as a whole, we need this flourishing diversity. A major reason deep learning has prospered and made breakthroughs up to today is that it has advanced through such diversity, right? items.question: How do you see the opportunities for university ML systems research given the gap in resources between academia and frontier AI labs?
items.object: Opportunities for academic ML systems research under resource constraints
items.answer: That is unavoidable, right? In some sense, universities certainly cannot do work at the scale of pre-training. But conversely, lack of resources—resource constraints—are also an opportunity to make people more creative. For example, why do we still insist on working on deep learning compilers? Because at a university I cannot have 100 people solving my problem. For a large company, having 100 people solve a problem in this direction is entirely normal. So we need to be creative. Conversely, universities offer space for you to do things in a more grounded, sustained way, so I think there are still many opportunities here. The second thing is collaboration with the open-source community. Universities cannot be isolated individuals; we need to produce work that the open-source community can help build together. Projects such as BLMSGLAM have driven the open-source community, and they also came from universities. In fact, many successful projects have a university presence behind them. Finally, in this ecosystem there are often opportunities—again, like the lesson of XGBoost—we find that you do not need to do everything, but you can do the things you consider critical and do them best. There are many modules in the entire LLM inference ecosystem. For example, doing the strongest kernel optimization does not require that much scale; you only need access to a latest NVIDIA GPU. At CMU, we recently also have the Flame Center, which can basically reach a cluster of around one hundred GPUs. With resources like that, compared with industry, you find that industry is often not that rich either—especially if you are in R&D rather than something else. At that point, it is not as well-funded as one might imagine. So I think there are still opportunities here.

items.question: How do you choose which ML systems research problems to work on?
items.object: Choosing ML systems research problems
items.answer: A lot of the time, for ML systems, when I work on something, I do not particularly think in terms of return on investment. Instead, I ask—at least I personally ask—where the bottleneck in this field is, and whether it can be solved. Of course, in that process we can identify problems. In particular, ML still has many vertical domains. For example, when we worked on agents, we found that structured-data generation in agents was very important: you need the output of the agent to be JSON, right, to satisfy a format. But current solutions do this poorly. That was our Ask Grandma project last year. As one module, it has become one of the de facto standards for structured generation in the open-source community, at least one of them. So there are many cases where you can identify bottlenecks in the real problem. That is one aspect. Second, I think you should also look at what problems you yourself are interested in, because different people choose different problems. We can just choose problems we are passionate about and can solve.

items.question: How do you view open source as an activity for university researchers and students?
items.object: Open source as a community activity and an approach to university research
items.answer: First, I think open source is a very good thing, right? People can communicate and share with one another in the community; sometimes people can star your code, right? And you can meet different people. So as a community activity, I think open source is very good. On the other hand, I think it is very important for universities, because universities alone do not easily make their work land in practice directly. You need to be able to share what you make with everyone and build it together. For students, I think open source is also a great opportunity. Usually, when you enter a company, you start by making a small component of a big project. Few people get an opportunity to architect something from scratch directly. If we did not do open-source projects, during a PhD there would be few chances to encounter this kind of opportunity to architect a large system. Universities also have the right soil for open source because, first, they are relatively neutral; second, open source often requires some spirit of contribution to the community. So in that respect, open source has its benefits. Of course, it brings overhead. It is not free: it means spending a lot of time looking at user feedback, fixing bugs, and interacting with the community. In the traditional sense, many of these things are not directly related to conventional research and paper writing, right? So not every group—indeed, probably very few groups—takes this route. But it is certainly one approach, I think.

items.question: How do you see the role of machine-learning compilation in OctoML’s evolving business model?

items.answer: Octo’s business model changed. At the beginning, when we first came out, large models were not yet so popular.
